title: Everything Dies: Secret Wars
subtitle: Jonathan Hickman's Marvel run
blurb: 250 issues from Fantastic Four #570 through Secret Wars #9, in the order they're meant to be read.
notes: 1 is essential, 2 is strongly recommended (the Fantastic Four run — it's what makes the ending land), 3 is genuinely optional. The minimum viable path is Tier 1 alone.

Most issues link to their series page rather than the issue, because Marvel only exposes the 20 most recent issues of any series to the outside world. The issue numbers tell you when to switch titles, which is the real difficulty with an interleaved run.
Reading order compiled from Comic Book Herald, Crushing Krisis and How To Love Comics; the Fantastic Four/FF weave follows the order Hickman specified for the omnibus.

sections.title: S.H.I.E.L.D.
sections.sub: 2010–2011 · come back to it later, but it rules

items.note: the back half was heavily delayed

sections.intro:
This one rules. It is dense, it is complicated, and it sits off to one side of everything else here — so leaving it until later costs you nothing, and picking it up cold is genuinely hard going.

Come back for it though. It is one of the coolest comic series anyone has made.

sections.title: Secret Warriors
sections.intro:
Nick Fury ran the world’s intelligence apparatus for decades. In the events just before this, he lost it — S.H.I.E.L.D. was dismantled after an alien infiltration was found to have reached the top of it, and what replaced it answered to someone worse.

So Fury goes underground and builds his own thing instead: off the books, staffed with young people whose powers nobody has on file.

None of that backstory is required. This is a spy comic that happens to share an author.

sections.title: Prelude — Dark Reign
sections.sub: start here · where the Fantastic Four run begins

items.note: Hickman’s story only — the earliest chapter here

sections.intro:
You don’t need to have read anything before this — but two things have just happened.

A superhuman registration law tore the hero community in half, and Reed Richards was one of its architects. By any reasonable measure, he was wrong. It cost him friendships, and for a while it cost him his marriage.

Then an alien infiltration of Earth ended with Norman Osborn shooting the invading queen on live television. He was rewarded with control of the country’s entire security apparatus — which he has spent the months since dismantling and rebuilding in his own image, with his own Avengers.

So: Osborn runs national security, and has opinions about who else should be allowed to. And Reed Richards is privately certain he made the worst call of his life. Rather than sit with that, he starts building a machine to ask every other version of himself how they would have handled it.

Six years of story come out of that one decision.

sections.title: Ultimate lead-in
sections.intro:
This is a different universe, and it’s supposed to feel that way.

From 2000, Marvel ran a parallel line retelling its characters from scratch for new readers — same names, no continuity baggage, harder edges. By the time Hickman arrives, that world has been through a catastrophe that killed a large share of its heroes, and its Spider-Man has died and been replaced by a teenager most readers hadn’t met.

The one thing worth carrying forward: this world’s Reed Richards is not the man you’ve been reading about. He went somewhere very dark in books that aren’t listed here, and he now calls himself the Maker.

Remember the name. It’s the part the main story eventually needs.

sections.title: Ultimate Comics: The Ultimates
sections.sub: establishes the Maker — pays off much later
sections.intro: Same parallel universe as the previous section. If you skipped that one, the only thing to carry in is that this world’s Reed Richards turned villain some time ago and goes by the Maker now.

sections.title: Avengers × New Avengers, part one

items.note: “Everything dies” — the best opening issue of the saga
where the book’s central moral problem grows teeth

sections.intro:
Two things happened just before this that aren’t in this list.

The Avengers and the X-Men fought a war over a returning cosmic force. It ended badly for everyone, with the X-Men’s founder dead and the hero community trusting itself less than it had in years. Hickman’s first issue opens in that aftermath — which is why the team is being rebuilt from scratch, and rebuilt enormous.

The second is older and quieter. Years ago a handful of the most powerful men in the Marvel Universe — Iron Man, Reed Richards, Namor, Black Bolt, Doctor Strange, Professor X — formed a private group to make the decisions nobody had elected them to make. They called themselves the Illuminati. It went badly enough that they stopped. New Avengers #1 is about them starting again.

You’ve seen these people be heroes. This is the book about what they do when no one is watching.

sections.title: Time Runs Out
sections.sub: an eight-month jump · the strongest sustained stretch
sections.intro:
The story jumps forward eight months, and two people return changed for reasons that happened in other books.

Steve Rogers is old. A villain drained the super-soldier serum out of him over in his own title, and he aged into the man he would have been had he never been frozen. Sam Wilson — the Falcon — carries the shield now.

Tony Stark is wrong. A magical event inverted the moral compass of a number of heroes and villains. Most were changed back. Tony preferred it, and arranged to stay that way.

Neither is explained on the page, and neither is worth reading first. But if you hit these issues wondering whether you missed something: you didn’t.

sections.title: Secret Wars
sections.sub: 2015 · with Siege and Thors woven in

items.note: the one tie-in most guides call necessary

sections.intro:
Two miniseries run alongside the main book and are woven in below. They aren’t bonus material — they were published concurrently and are paced to sit between its issues.

Siege is the one most guides call outright necessary: it covers the defence of Battleworld’s border, which the main series treats as already understood. Thors is a police procedural set in the same world — skippable in the strict sense, but it’s the best-executed tie-in of the event and it lands harder here than it would afterwards.

The remaining several dozen Secret Wars tie-ins are self-contained stories set in other corners of Battleworld. None of them are needed.

sections.title: Coda — Ultimate End
sections.intro: Bendis and Bagley, who launched the Ultimate line in 2000, were given the job of closing it. It is widely considered a disappointment, and it doesn’t connect to Hickman’s plot. Listed for completeness rather than recommended.
